claims.text: Engineering a heterostructured microstructure with a bimodal or gradient grain-size distribution concurrently improves strength and ductility.
Interfacial strain gradients in heterostructured microstructures provide additional strain hardening.
Combining fine, strong grain regions with coarse, ductile grain regions enables simultaneous strength and ductility.
Conventional metallic alloys with homogeneous microstructures exhibit a typical trade-off between strength and ductility.
Controlled thermal or mechanical treatments can produce bimodal or gradient grain structures.
Load-bearing applications require alloys possessing both high strength and ductility under ambient loading conditions.
Interfaces between coarse and fine grains constitute the structural mediator of the proposed improvement.
Alternating regions with different grain sizes generate interfacial strain gradients during deformation.
The resulting interfacial strain gradients increase the strain-hardening rate.
Additional strain hardening delays necking and failure.
The heterostructured arrangement maintains enhanced overall strength while delaying failure.
Heterostructured samples will show statistically significant simultaneous increases in tensile strength and ductility relative to homogeneous samples.
Uniform grain refinement and precipitation hardening typically enhance strength at the expense of ductility.
Strong interfacial bonding is required for the proposed strength–ductility improvement.
The gradient or bimodal grain-size distribution must be optimally engineered for the improvement to occur.
Performance is sensitive to processing conditions and may vary with temperature or strain rate.
The proposed trend is supported by mechanistic considerations and multiscale simulation insights.
The magnitude of the improvements and the optimal microstructural configuration remain quantitatively unestablished.
